records.excerpt: Title: Goldman Sachs (GS) Q2 2026 Earnings Preview: $14.47 EPS Expected, OpenAI IPO Candidacy, and the $1,067 Triangle Trigger URL Source: http://www.tradingkey.com/analysis/stocks/us-stocks/262028603-goldman-sachs-gs-q2-2026-earnings-preview-triangle-breakout-1067-tradingkey Published Time: 2026-07-14T13:00:00+00:00 Markdown Content: TradingKey - Goldman Sachs Group (NYSE: [GS](https://www.tradingkey.com/markets/stocks/nasdaq-gs)) is set to announce its second-quarter 2026 results ahead of the market open this morning, July 14, 2026. The initial release is at 7:00 AM ET, followed by the conference call at 8:30 AM ET. Prior to the announcement, analysts had projected a Q2 2026 adjusted Earnings Per Share (EPS) of $14.20 to $14.47, or about 32% higher than last year's Q2 figures of $10.91, on total revenues of $15.9 billion to $16.49 billion, compared to $14.58 billion last year. Goldman has surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate in each of the past four quarters, boasting an average EPS surprise of 13.10%. Currently, options are betting on an implied move of roughly 4.78% in either direction. The stock is currently trading at $1,047, within a symmetrical triangle and with an RSI approaching 50. A breakout above $1,067 would target $1,096 and $1,123, whereas a breakdown below $1,029 would expose the 200-period EMA at $1,014. ## Why Q2 2026 Consensus Is Significantly Lower Than Q1 The $14.20 to $14.47 EPS range for the second quarter is down sharply from the record of $17.55 EPS reported in the first quarter. First quarter performance saw a sharp spike in total revenues to $17.23 billion from $14.58 billion the year before, an uptick analysts attributed to a rebound in equity trading. The second quarter consensus revenue forecast of $15.9 billion to $16.49 billion is below the $17.23 billion seen in the first quarter, or a sequential drop in total revenues of 7% to 8%, mostly as the trading environment normalizes. The eight-thirty conference call will help investors determine if (1) investment banking fee revenue grew from the first quarter's strong recovery or if it started losing traction; (2) if the Asset & Wealth Management business can continue its first quarter growth of $4.08 billion, which was up 10% over the same period last year; (3) whether equities revenue normalised from Q1’s $5.33 billion toward the $4.0 to $4.5 billion range that would be consistent with a less-volatile Q2 trading environment, and; (4) whether operating expenses as a percentage of revenue declined from Q1’s $10.43 billion, which at 60.5% efficiency ratio left room for improvement. Goldman has beaten Zacks estimates by 13.10% over the past four quarters; a similar upside against a $14.47 EPS consensus puts second quarter adjusted earnings close to $16.36. ## OpenAI IPO Lead, the $70 Billion Mandate Wins, and a 19-Year High in EMEA M&A Three factors ahead of today's release help frame the medium term revenue outlook outside of the second quarter print. Goldman's M&A in EMEA reached its highest point in 19 years in the first half of 2026, accounting for 44% of all deal value in the region, and confirms that Goldman is taking a larger share of M&A deals in the most lucrative deal environment since 2007. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are among the two leading prospects to manage the anticipated OpenAI Initial Public Offering (IPO), which would be a source of underwriting revenues that would be in excess of any normal quarter's equity underwriting. Goldman's equity underwriting revenues in the first quarter were $535 million; the OpenAI mandate, should it go through as projected, could produce fee revenues that dwarf this quarterly figure, making it the most significant single event to impact Goldman's third or fourth quarter consensus forecasts. Goldman's Verizon and Lockheed Martin Institutional Retirement Plan mandates, totaling some $70 billion, would be the first tangible milestone of the company's 2030 target for $750 billion in asset under management in the AWM business line, set by David Solomon. Are SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic’s IPOs Draining Bitcoin liquidity? Jul 14, 2026 119 Bitcoin blockchain Crypto ETF Table of Contents Toggle No single force explains it. Bitcoin fell sharply as SpaceX went public and Anthropic and OpenAI prepared their own listings, and crypto ETFs recorded record outflows in the same window. But the drop was also driven by a broader risk-off shift, a hawkish Fed, and arbitrage unwinding unrelated to the IPOs. Key Takeaways SpaceX’s IPO, the largest in history, landed in the same weeks Bitcoin fell sharply, and OpenAI and Anthropic listings could add over $200 billion more in new equity supply. Spot Bitcoin ETFs posted record monthly outflows during this period, which some analysts tied directly to capital rotating into the IPOs. Altcoins fell harder than Bitcoin, which fits the pattern of investors liquidating their most volatile holdings first when raising cash. Whether this is a temporary reallocation or a lasting shift away from crypto investment will show up in ETF flows and altcoin performance over the coming months. What Actually Happened? SpaceX went public in June 2026 in what became the largest IPO on record, raising tens of billions of dollars at a valuation north of $1.7 trillion. OpenAI and Anthropic are expected to follow with listings of their own, and combined, this cluster of mega-IPOs could pull more than $200 billion in fresh equity supply into the market by the end of the year. In the same window, Bitcoin fell hard, dropping toward the $58,000-$60,000 range after trading near its 2026 highs earlier in the year. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded their worst month of net outflows since the products launched, and altcoins underperformed Bitcoin by a wide margin. The timing was close enough that a narrative formed almost immediately: investors were pulling money out of crypto to fund allocations in the SpaceX IPO, with OpenAI and Anthropic expected to extend the same pattern. That narrative is plausible on its face. Whether it holds up depends on separating correlation from causation, which is harder than the headlines suggest. Why an IPO Could Pull Money Out of Crypto? The logic behind the drain theory rests on one basic fact: an IPO does not create new money. It transfers capital that already exists from investors into a newly public company. To buy into a hot listing, investors need cash on hand, and they typically raise it by selling something they already own. Crypto is an easy target for that kind of selling. It trades 24/7, moves fast, and can be liquidated in minutes when someone needs capital quickly. A few specific channels reinforce this idea. Retail investors chasing IPO allocations overlap heavily with retail crypto holders, so some of the buying power for SpaceX shares plausibly came directly from crypto positions. Once a company the size of SpaceX enters major indices, index funds are forced to buy in, and they often raise the cash by trimming other holdings. Institutions holding Bitcoin through ETFs also face pressure to rebalance toward the IPO opportunity rather than sit on existing crypto exposure. The Evidence Supporting the Drain Theory The market data gives this theory real support, not just a coincidence of timing. Around the SpaceX listing, Bitcoin dropped by roughly 20% from recent levels. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed about $4.5 billion in June 2026 alone, their heaviest monthly outflow since the products launched in January 2024, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for the bulk of it. The pattern extended beyond Bitcoin ETF flows. Space and AI-adjacent equities rallied in the same stretch that crypto weakened, suggesting money was moving from one asset class into the other. Altcoins also fell harder than Bitcoin, which is consistent with investors liquidating their most volatile, easiest-to-sell positions first when they need cash on short notice. The Case Against a Clean Cause-and-Effect Story The counter-argument is just as well-documented. Fabian Dori, chief investment officer at Sygnum, has pointed out that the ETF outflow pattern lines up more closely with the unwinding of cash-and-carry arbitrage trades than with a genuine rotation into equities. In this trade, institutions hold Bitcoin spot positions while shorting Bitcoin futures to capture a pricing gap. When that gap narrows, traders close both sides, which shows up as an ETF outflow even though nobody involved is turning bearish on Bitcoin or reallocating toward the SpaceX IPO. Supporting that view, exchange balances and stablecoin supply stayed largely stable through the period, which would be unusual if investors were broadly cashing out of crypto to fund equity purchases. Riskier crypto products also kept attracting inflows during the same stretch, which cuts against the idea of a wholesale exit from the asset class. At the same time, the broader market was under pressure for reasons that had nothing to do with any IPO. Equities sold off sharply on AI bubble concerns, geopolitical tension pushed oil prices higher, and a hawkish Federal Reserve kept rate-cut expectations low. Bitcoin trades as a high-beta risk asset in conditions like these, and it would likely have fallen even without a single IPO on the calendar. What This Means for a Crypto Investment Strategy? The honest takeaway is that both stories are partly right, and neither fully explains what happened. The IPO wave is large enough to matter, and the timing of the ETF outflows lines up with it closely enough to be a genuine factor. But arbitrage unwinding and macro pressure were clearly at work too, and untangling the exact weight of each is not something the current data supports with confidence. For anyone building a crypto investment approach around this event, the more useful question is not “did the IPOs cause the drop” but “is this pressure temporary or structural. An IPO is a one-time reallocation of capital, not a permanent shift in how much money exists. If the selling was driven mainly by IPO funding needs, it should ease once SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic allocations are settled, and some of that capital could rotate back into crypto. If the selling was driven mainly by macro conditions, crypto could stay under pressure regardless of how the IPOs play out, since a hawkish Fed and weak risk appetite would weigh on Bitcoin either way. This is also why long-term Bitcoin investment decisions are rarely well served by reacting to a single month of ETF flow data, especially when the same data is open to more than one credible explanation. What to Watch Next? A few signals will clarify which story is winning. ETF flow direction is the clearest one: a return to sustained inflows would suggest capital is coming back, while continued outflows would support the ongoing-drain case. The timing of the OpenAI and Anthropic listings matters too, since a wide gap between them would spread out any funding pressure, while a tight cluster would concentrate it. The altcoin-versus-Bitcoin spread is another useful indicator. If altcoins start recovering ahead of Bitcoin once the IPO allocations are digested, that would point to the forced-selling phase ending. If they continue to underperform for months after the listings close, it would suggest something more structural is going on beyond a one-time reallocation. Conclusion The idea that SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic’s IPOs are draining crypto’s liquidity is not a myth, but it is not the full story either. records.title: Apple Launches Thermonuclear Lawsuit Against OpenAI Over Secrets
records.excerpt: Apple has filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging a former executive stole critical trade secrets to develop a rival AI hardware device. In a dramatic escalation of the artificial intelligence arms race, Apple has fired a devastating legal salvo at OpenAI, filing a sweeping lawsuit that alleges a senior executive at the AI startup orchestrated a monthslong campaign to steal highly classified hardware trade secrets. The aggressive litigation, authorized by CEO Tim Cook in one of his final major acts before transitioning power to successor John Ternus, represents a massive defensive maneuver aimed at crippling a direct threat to the iPhone's two-decade dominance of the consumer tech market.The high-stakes corporate warfare carries immense implications for the global technology ecosystem. As multinational giants battle for supremacy in the emerging hardware landscape, the downstream effects will dictate how AI is integrated into consumer devices globally. For emerging tech hubs in Nairobi, Lagos, and Cape Town, the outcome of this lawsuit could fundamentally alter the regulatory frameworks governing intellectual property, engineering talent poaching, and the future architecture of mobile computing platforms across the continent.Echoes of the Android WarIndustry analysts are universally comparing the lawsuit to the late Steve Jobs' infamous 2010 declaration of "thermonuclear war" against Google's Android operating system, which he fiercely branded a stolen product. Apple is utilizing the exact same playbook, betting that aggressive, protracted litigation can legally entangle OpenAI, thereby delaying the startup from successfully launching a proprietary, AI-powered consumer device that could render the traditional smartphone obsolete.The lawsuit, filed late Friday, specifically targets a senior OpenAI executive who previously held a top-tier position within Apple's elite product design team. Apple's legal filings assert that the executive utilized their deep institutional knowledge and existing relationships to siphon confidential engineering schematics, proprietary supply chain data, and critical design frameworks to OpenAI. Apple claims this intellectual property theft was executed specifically to accelerate OpenAI's highly secretive internal efforts to build dedicated AI hardware devices.The Race Beyond the SmartphoneThe friction between the two titans occurs at a highly volatile inflection point for the technology sector. The industry is aggressively racing to develop the next dominant computing paradigm—devices powered natively by large language models that do not rely on traditional application ecosystems. Whoever successfully designs and commercializes this post-smartphone hardware will inherit a consumer market worth trillions of dollars, effectively dictating the terms of global digital interaction for the next twenty years.Apple currently commands a market capitalization nearing $3.5 trillion (KES 458 trillion), heavily reliant on the continued supremacy of the iPhone hardware cycle.OpenAI, led by CEO Sam Altman, has recently been valued at over $80 billion and is actively attempting to transition from software APIs to physical consumer devices.Altman responded directly to the litigation on the social platform X, stating, "I am not afraid of Apple, but I have tremendous respect for them."The lawsuit has also reignited the fierce, long-standing public feud between Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.Strategic Litigation as a Business MoatWhile the precise evidentiary basis of Apple's claims remains shielded under corporate confidentiality, the timing of the lawsuit is undeniably strategic. The suit lands before OpenAI has formally announced or released any physical product, effectively forcing the startup to divert immense financial resources and executive focus toward legal defense rather than product development. By attacking OpenAI's hardware ambitions in their infancy, Apple aims to maintain its absolute stranglehold on the mobile computing ecosystem while simultaneously rushing its own AI-integrated hardware to the market.The legal confrontation also highlights the intense, ruthless competition for elite engineering talent in Silicon Valley. With the boundaries between hardware design and artificial intelligence software rapidly dissolving, companies are aggressively deploying non-disclosure agreements and trade secret litigation to lock down human capital. If Apple succeeds in proving corporate espionage, it could result in massive financial damages and devastating legal injunctions that would permanently bar OpenAI from utilizing the disputed technology in any future consumer device.The Future of Global Tech SupremacyAs the legal battle moves into the federal courts, the entire technology sector will be watching closely. Apple's thermonuclear response confirms that the company views OpenAI not merely as a software partner or API provider, but as an existential threat to its hardware empire. The ruling in this case will not only determine the immediate trajectory of both companies but will permanently redefine the legal boundaries of innovation, talent mobility, and corporate warfare in the artificial intelligence era.

OpenAIは2026年7月9日（米国時間）、ChatGPT の役割を質問への回答から業務の遂行へと広げる新機能「ChatGPT Work」と、Codexを統合した新しいChatGPTデスクトップアプリを発表した。 ChatGPT Workは発表当日よりWebとモバイルのChatGPT でPro、Enterprise、Edu向けに利用が可能になり、PlusとBusinessには今後数日程度で展開される。ChatGPTデスクトップアプリは WindowsとMac向けに世界中でダウンロードが可能。同アプリではチャット、ワーク、CodexをFreeを含むすべてのプランで利用できる。 今回の発表は、ChatGPTの体験を「質問に答える」から、「業務や成果物作成を支援する」体験へと広げるものだ。 本稿では、その概要を同社リリースをベースにお伝えする。 どこにいてもタスクを進行、デスクトップでさらに活用 ChatGPT Workは、どこにいてもタスクを前に進められるように設計されている。スマートフォンからタスクを始めるよう依頼したり、あるいは移動中にドラフトをチェック、会議の合間に長時間実行中のワークフローの状況を確認することができる。帰社すれば同じ作業をWebで引き継具ことができる。 デスクトップでは、ChatGPTがローカルファイルやアプリを使って仕事を進行。Web ベースの作業では、ChatGPTの新しい内蔵ブラウザがWebサイト、ツール、オンラインファイルを取り込み、作業を進める場所を1つにまとめる。 Codexアプリは新しいChatGPTデスクトップアプリに統合された。Codexは、開発者や技術専門職向けの強力なコーディングエージェントであることはそのままに、差分内でのインライン編集、サイドパネルでのプルリクエストレビュー、より高速なコンピューター操作（GPT‑5.6 搭載）、1 つのプロジェクトでの複数リポジトリ対応など、主要なワークフロー全体で新機能を備えた。 ■アプリやワークフローからスライド、シート、ドキュメント、サイトを作成 ChatGPT Workを始めるには、プラグインを使って、普段の作業で使っているツールや関連情報を連携させる。 プラグインは、Slack、Microsoft Teams、Google Drive、SharePoint、メール、カレンダー、CRM、プロジェクトトラッカー、その他の社内ツールなどのアプリやシステムに ChatGPTを接続する。 ChatGPT は、プロンプトに基づいてプラグインを参照すべきタイミングを自動的に判断していく。また、プロンプトに「@」に続けてアプリ名を入力すれば、特定のアプリからコンテキストを取得するよう ChatGPT に直接指示することもできる。 新しい統合プラグインディレクトリにより、プラグインが1か所にまとまり、ChatGPT は会話中に関連するプラグインを提案できる。 アプリやツールを接続すると、ChatGPT はユーザーが何をしようとしているかを理解して、関連するソースから情報を取り込み、ドキュメント、デッキ、分析を作成。ユーザーが主導権を保ったまま、バックグラウンドで下書きを磨き続ける。 反復作業を任せて、より重要な仕事に集中 ChatGPT Workは反復作業を肩代わりして、より大きな成果につながる仕事に集中できるように支援を行なう。 スケジュール済みタスクでは、ChatGPT にアクションを1回だけ実行させたり、スケジュールやイベント発生時に繰り返し実行させたり、時間の経過に伴う変化を監視させることが可能だ。 スケジュール済みタスクは、接続済みのアプリやブラウザを使って次のことを実行する。 ・毎週の Slack 更新を確認し、定例会議のアジェンダを更新 ・毎朝 Web サイトとダッシュボードを確認し、変更点を要約してレポートを送信 ・新しい顧客フィードバックを監視し、繰り返し見られるテーマを優先度の高いプロダクトアイデアに変換 ・メールで新しいフィードバックが届いたらプレゼンテーションを更新 Web とデスクトップアプリを横断して、仕事をより速く進める デスクトップ版の ChatGPT には内蔵ブラウザが加わり、オンラインでの情報収集、Web ベースのツールの利用、Web 上の作業の改善を1か所で行なえるようになった。 市場調査、情報源の比較、Web サイトからの情報取得、Google WorkspaceやMicrosoft 365のファイルをアプリ内で開いて改善する作業をChatGPT に依頼できる。 ChatGPTはブラウザを使って最新のコンテキストを取り込み、Web ページをまたいで手順を実行。ユーザーが確認して指示する間も作業を進められる。 デスクトップでは、Computer Useにより、ChatGPTがユーザーに代わってコンピューターを操作。アプリ、ツール、ブラウザをまたいで、クリック、入力、必要な場所へのファイル移動などのタスクをバックグラウンドで実行する。 records.excerpt: GPT-Liveとは？OpenAI最新音声モデルの仕組み・使い方・料金を解説 DXを推進するAIポータルメディア「AIsmiley」｜ AI製品・サービスの比較・検索サイト サイトの使い方 情報提供はこちらから 掲載希望の企業様へ 03-6452-4750 10:00〜18:00 年末年始除く AI活用を無料相談 AI・人工知能のAIsmiley TOP ニュース GPT-Liveとは？OpenAI最新音声モデルの仕組み・使い方・料金を解説 GPT-Liveとは？OpenAI最新音声モデルの仕組み・使い方・料金を解説 最終更新日:2026/07/13 GPT-Liveは、 OpenAI が2026年7月8日に発表した新世代の音声モデルです。聞きながら話せるフルデュプレックス構造の仕組み、Advanced Voice Modeとの違い、プラン別の料金と提供範囲、法人利用の可否、音声データの扱いまで、公式情報をもとに解説します。 OpenAIが新しい音声モデルを発表して以来、「GPT-Liveって結局なにが変わったの？」「自分のプランで使えるの？」「Advanced Voice Modeとどう違うの？」という声が増えています。 一言でいえば、 ChatGPT の音声機能を根本から作り替えるアップデートがGPT-Liveです。聞くことと話すことを同時に行えるため、これまでの「交互に話す」やり取りから、人と話しているような会話へと一気に近づきました。 本記事では、GPT-Liveの仕組みと進化点、プラン別の料金と提供範囲を、OpenAIの公式情報をもとに整理します。さらに、法人向けワークスペースでは提供開始時点で利用できないという事実も取り上げています。読み終えるころには、自社や自分の環境でGPT-Liveを使えるかどうかを判断できるはずです。 GPT-Liveとは？OpenAIが発表した新世代の音声モデル GPT-Live（GPT Liveとも表記されます）とは、ChatGPTの音声機能「ChatGPT Voice」を刷新する新世代の音声モデルです。最大の特徴は、聞きながら同時に話せる点にあります。 OpenAIは現地時間2026年7月8日（日本時間7月9日）にGPT-Liveを発表しました。iOS・Android・ChatGPT.comのWeb版に向けて、世界中で順次展開されています。 現在、ChatGPTのVoiceやDictation（音声入力）といった機能は、週に1億5,000万人以上に利用されています。その体験全体が変わるという意味で、今回のアップデートのインパクトは小さくありません。 GPT-Live-1とGPT-Live-1 miniの違い 提供されるモデルは2種類です。 GPT-Live-1：有料プラン（Go・Plus・Pro）で標準となる上位モデル GPT-Live-1 mini：無料プランで標準となる軽量モデル つまり、無料プランでもGPT-Liveの体験そのものは利用できます。ただし提供範囲の重要な条件は、後述の「料金と対応プラン」の比較表で解説します。 APIでの提供も予定されており、開発者や企業は公式フォームから通知の登録が可能です。 出典： Introducing GPT-Live｜OpenAI GPT-Liveの仕組み｜「全二重」と「委譲」という2つの転換 GPT-Liveの本質は、「連続的なインタラクション」と「深い処理の分離」という2つのアーキテクチャ変更にあります。順番に見ていきましょう。 連続的なインタラクション（フルデュプレックス） GPT-Liveは、フルデュプレックス（全二重）というアーキテクチャで構築されています。フルデュプレックスとは、聞くことと話すことを同時に行える方式のことです。 従来のように「メッセージのかたまり」を順番に処理するのではなく、GPT-Liveは入力を受け取りながら出力を生成し続けます。そのため「話すか」「聞き続けるか」「一時停止するか」「割り込むか」「ツールを呼び出すか」といった判断を、1秒間に何度も下せるのです。 この設計から、次のような振る舞いが生まれます。 「mhmm（うんうん）」「yeah（うん）」といった相槌で、聞いていることを示す ユーザーが考えをまとめている間は、割り込まずに黙って待つ リアルタイム翻訳のように、聞きながら訳す処理をこなす 深い処理の「委譲」（delegation） 2つ目の転換が、会話を担う部分と重い処理を担う部分の切り離しです。 Web検索や深い推論、複雑な作業が必要な質問を受けると、GPT-Liveはそのタスクを別のモデルに委譲（delegation）します。提供開始時点で裏側に置かれているのは GPT-5.5 。今後フロンティアモデルが更新されるたびに、裏側のモデルも継続的に差し替えられる予定です。 重要なのは、委譲している間も会話が止まらないこと。裏で検索や推論が走っている間も、GPT-Liveはユーザーと話し続けます。結果として、気まずい沈黙が生まれません。 従来方式との違い GPT-Liveが何を解決したのかは、過去の2方式と並べると分かりやすくなります。 方式 代表例 仕組み 抱えていた課題 カスケード型 初代ChatGPT Voice 音声認識（STT）→LLM→音声合成（TTS）を直列に接続 モデル間で情報が失われ、応答が遅くぎこちない ターン制 Advanced Voice Mode 単一モデル内で音声を処理・生成 沈黙で発話の終わりを判定するため、短い間や背景ノイズで誤って割り込む 全二重 GPT-Live 入力処理と出力生成を同時並行 提供開始時点では動画・画面共有に非対応 出典： Introducing GPT-Live｜OpenAI GPT-Liveでできること｜ChatGPT Voiceの主な進化点 GPT-Liveが搭載されたChatGPT Voiceの進化は、大きく4つに整理できます。「自然な会話」「賢い回答」「聞き上手」「ビジュアル表示」です。 より自然な会話になる 話している途中で割り込んで質問する、考えをまとめるために少し黙る、「もう少しゆっくり話して」と頼む。こうした操作が自然にできるようになりました。 ChatGPTの側も「mhmm」「got it（わかった）」といった短い言葉で相槌を打ちます。会話についてきていることが、声から伝わる仕組みです。 音声そのものも刷新されました。ChatGPTに用意された9種類の音声が、GPT-Live向けにリマスターされています。内訳はArbor、Breeze、Cove、Ember、Juniper、Maple、Sol、Spruce、Valeです。 なお、あらかじめ用意されたChatGPTのパーソナリティ（性格プリセット）は、現時点ではLiveに適用されません。会話中に口調やテンポを指示する形になります。 推論レベルをInstant・Medium・Highから選べる 回答の深さは、用途に応じて切り替えられます。 Instant ：素早い応答が欲しいとき Medium／High ：じっくり考えさせたいとき 具体的なモデルの割り当ては以下の通りです。GPT-Live-1 InstantとGPT-Live-1 miniはGPT-5.5 Instantを、GPT-Live-1 MediumとHighはGPT-5.5 Thinkingを中〜高の推論強度で使用します。 設定方法は「設定→音声→Intelligence」からです。ただしこの項目はアカウントによって表示されない場合があり、選べるレベルもプランによって異なります。推論レベルを上げると、特にWeb検索を伴う場面で応答までの時間は長くなる点に留意してください。 話しながら画面に情報が出る（ビジュアルカード） 音声だけでは伝わりにくい情報もあります。GPT-Liveでは、会話の最中に天気・株価・スポーツなどのトピックについて、リッチなビジュアルカードを画面に表示できるようになりました。 Web検索、メモリ、画像の扱いにも引き続き対応します。会話中に画像を添付したり、話せない場面ではテキストで入力したりと、同じチャットの中で音声とテキストを行き来できる設計です。 聞き取りの精度が上がった ユーザーが少し黙っても、ChatGPTはすぐに割り込まなくなりました。会話の冒頭で「私が聞くまで待って」と伝えれば、黙って聞き続けます。 通り過ぎる車の音や近くの話し声といった背景ノイズがあっても、ユーザーの声に集中しやすくなった点も改善のひとつ。移動中や屋外での利用を想定した進化と言えるでしょう。 このほか、Apple CarPlayでの音声会話や、他のアプリを使いながら会話を継続する「バックグラウンド会話」といった設定も用意されています。 出典： Introducing GPT-Live｜OpenAI ／ ChatGPT Voice｜OpenAI Help Center GPT-Liveの性能｜Advanced Voice Modeとの比較 GPT-Liveは、人間による評価と各種ベンチマークの双方で、従来のAdvanced Voice Modeを上回りました。 OpenAIは会話の心地よさと流れを測る新しい人間評価を設計しています。5〜10分の会話を対象にした比較では、総合的な好ましさ、発話の受け渡し、割り込み、会話の流れ、やり取りの自然さのいずれにおいても、GPT-Live-1とGPT-Live-1 miniがAdvanced Voice Modeより強く好まれました。 ベンチマークの結果は次のとおりです。 ベンチマーク 測定する内容 結果 GPQA 生物・化学・物理における専門家レベルの科学的推論 GPT-Live-1がAdvanced Voice Modeを大幅に上回る BrowseComp エージェント的なWeb検索と、見つけにくい情報を探し出す能力 GPT-Live-1が明確なスコア向上 τ³-Voice Telecom（社内版） 現実的な複数ターンの通信サポート業務 GPT-Live-1がAdvanced Voice Modeを上回る ただし、この性能向上をどう解釈するかには議論があります。スコアの伸びは音声対話層そのものの進化というより、裏側でGPT-5.5に処理を委譲していることに由来する部分が大きいのではないか、と指摘する声も一部のメディアから出ています。この点についてOpenAIは公式に見解を示していません。 出典： Introducing GPT-Live｜OpenAI ／ GPT-Live System Card｜OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub GPT-Liveの料金と対応プラン｜無料でも使えるのか 結論から言うと、GPT-Liveは無料プランでも使えます。GPT-Live自体に追加料金はなく、ChatGPTの各プランに含まれる形で提供されます。 ただし、使えるモデルはプランによって異なります。そして法人向けワークスペースは、提供開始時点では対象外です。 プラン 標準で使えるモデル 提供開始時点の状況 Free GPT-Live-1 mini 利用可（順次展開） Go / Plus / Pro GPT-Live-1 利用可（順次展開） Business ― 利用不可 Enterprise ― 利用不可 Edu ― 利用不可 ※OpenAI公式ヘルプセンターに基づきます。提供条件は変更される可能性があるため、最新の情報は公式サイトをご確認ください。 対応環境はChatGPTのWeb版とiOS・Androidアプリです。加えて、次の環境では提供開始時点でLiveを利用できません。 一時チャット（Temporary Chats） ChatGPTデスクトップアプリ Work Codex カスタムGPTs 音声機能の利用上限はプランと音声オプションによって異なり、変更される場合もあります。上限に近づくと、ChatGPT上に通知が表示される仕組みです。 出典： ChatGPT Voice｜OpenAI Help Center ／ Introducing GPT-Live｜OpenAI 法人でGPT-Liveは使えるのか？導入前に確認すべき3つのこと ここが本記事で最もお伝えしたい部分です。ChatGPT Business・Enterprise・Eduのワークスペースでは、提供開始時点でGPT-Liveを利用できません。 法人利用を検討している場合、まず確認すべきは自社の契約形態です。 ①法人向けワークスペースは提供開始時点で対象外 「無料版を含むすべてのユーザーが利用可能」と報じている記事も見かけますが、これは個人向けプランに限った話です。OpenAIの公式ヘルプセンターには、Business・Enterprise・Eduのワークスペースでは提供開始時点でGPT-Liveが利用できず、該当プランのユーザーは従来通りの音声オプションを継続して利用する旨が明記されています。 ここを取り違えると、社内展開の計画そのものが狂いかねません。加えてLiveは段階的な展開のため、プラン・地域・ワークスペース・アプリのバージョンによって表示が異なります。 ②音声データはどう扱われるのか 情報システム部門や法務部門が気にするのは、音声データの扱いでしょう。公式ヘルプセンターの記述を整理します。 LiveおよびAdvancedの音声クリップは、チャット履歴に表示される文字起こしとあわせて保存され、保持期間は30日 チャットを削除すると、関連する音声クリップも30日以内に削除される（セキュリティ・安全・法令上の理由がある場合を除く） アーカイブはサイドバーから消えるだけで、チャットもクリップも削除されない 音声クリップは、ユーザーが明示的に共有を選ばない限りモデルの学習には使われない ただし「Improve the model for everyone」がオンの場合、プランと設定によっては文字起こしなどが学習に使われる場合がある Business・Enterprise・Eduのワークスペースでは、音声クリップを学習用に共有すること自体ができない なお、OpenAIはデータ保持について、法的手続きの影響を受ける可能性がある旨を公式ヘルプセンターに注記しています。最新の条件は必ず公式サイトをご確認ください。 ③導入前チェックリスト 社内会議にそのまま持ち込める形で整理しました。 自社の契約は個人向けプランか、法人向けワークスペースか 音声クリップの30日保持は、自社の情報セキュリティ規程・データ保持ポリシーに抵触しないか 「Improve the model for everyone」の設定を、組織として統一できているか 会議や商談など、第三者の音声が入る場面での利用可否を定めたか 未成年の利用者がいる場合、ペアレンタルコントロールの方針を整理したか 動画・画面共有を伴う業務があるか（ある場合はAdvancedの併用が必要） 出典： ChatGPT Voice｜OpenAI Help Center Live・Advanced・Standardの使い分け｜「置き換え」ではない 「GPT-LiveがAdvanced Voice Modeを置き換える」という説明を見かけますが、これは正確ではありません。AdvancedもStandardも設定画面に残り、用途によって使い分ける形になります。 とくに動画や画面共有を使いたい場合は、今もAdvancedを選ぶ必要があります。 モード 位置づけ 動画・画面共有 主な用途 Live 最新の音声体験（GPT-Live搭載） 非対応 自然な対話、Web検索、メモリ、ビジュアル表示 Advanced 従来のリアルタイム音声体験 対応（対象プランのモバイルアプリ） 画面を見せながらの質疑、カスタムGPTsとの音声会話 Standard 発話を文字起こししてから応答する方式 ― Liveが使えない環境での代替 切り替えは「設定→音声（Settings→Voice）」から、Live・Advanced・Standardのいずれかを選ぶだけ。表示される選択肢は、プラン・地域・アプリのバージョンによって変わります。 カスタムGPTsとの音声会話も、Advanced経由であれば引き続き利用できます。その際、GPTsではShimmerという専用の音声が使われます。 GPT-Liveの制限と注意点 便利になった一方で、提供開始時点では5つの制限があります。 制限事項 内容 ①動画・画面共有 非対応 Liveでは動画や画面共有を使えません。連携アプリやプラグインも提供開始時点では対象外です。OpenAIは今後の対応を予定しています。 ②言語による品質差 GPT-LiveはChatGPTでよく使われる言語向けに最適化されており、言語によっては非ネイティブのアクセントや流暢さの不足が生じる可能性があります。 ③1対1会話向けの設計 Liveは基本的に1対1の会話を想定した設計です。背景ノイズには対応できるものの、複数話者の環境には最適化されておらず、人同士が話している声に反応してしまうことがあります。議事録用途を考えている方は注意してください。 ④API 未提供 APIでの提供は「近日中」とされており、現時点では自社サービスへの組み込みはできません。 ⑤相槌の多さへの指摘 初期のユーザーからは、相槌が多すぎてかえって会話の邪魔になる、という声も一部で報告されています。ここは公式の見解ではなく、あくまで利用者の感想として捉えてください。 音声ならではの安全対策 音声会話はリアルタイムで進むため、OpenAIは音声に固有の安全対策を用意しています。 危険な出力を検知した場合には、より安全な応答へ誘導する、支援リソースを表示する、リスクの高い場面では音声会話を終了する、といった仕組みが働きます。自傷に関する会話では、専門家が監修したクライシスヘルプラインの案内が行われます。 10代のユーザー向けには、年齢に応じた振る舞いをモデルに直接学習させました。保護者はペアレンタルコントロールで子どもの利用可否を決められ、自傷や自殺の意図が疑われる高リスクな状況では連携した保護者に通知が届く場合もあります。実在する人物の声を模倣しないための安全対策も導入済みです。 GPT-LiveとGemini Liveの違い リアルタイム音声AIの分野では、Googleの Gemini Liveが先行してきました。両者は「聞きながら話す」自然な会話という目標こそ共通しているものの、強みの置きどころが異なります。 観点 GPT-Live Gemini Live（Gemini 3.1 Flash Live） 設計思想 会話の自然さ＋裏側のフロンティアモデルへの委譲による「賢さ」 低遅延と多言語対応を軸にしたリアルタイム対話 動画・画面共有 提供開始時点では非対応 対応 API records.title: 「ChatGPTワーク」提供開始 Claude Coworkの対抗機能がついに登場
records.excerpt: 米OpenAIは7月9日（現地時間）、新しい業務用エージェント「ChatGPT Work」（ChatGPTワーク）を発表した。ChatGPTに組み込まれ、SlackやGoogle Driveなどの業務アプリやファイルを横断して自律的に作業する。目標を伝えるだけで、文書やスプレッドシート、プレゼンテーションなどを完成品として仕上げ、数時間に及ぶ複雑なプロジェクトにも継続して取り組めるという。 ChatGPTワーク ※クリックすると拡大画像が見られます ChatGPT Workは7月9日から、ウェブ版とiOS／Android版で段階的に提供を始めた。まずPro、Enterprise、Eduの各プランを対象とし、PlusとBusinessにも数日かけて拡大する。対象アカウントへの展開は順次行われるため、プランが対応していても、すぐには表示されない場合がある。 「プロンプト」ではなく「達成したい目的」を入力 同機能は、Claudeの「Cowork」に対する事実上の対抗機能といえる。プロンプトごとに回答を返す従来の「チャット」とは異なり、最新モデル「GPT-5.6」を頭脳に、「Codex」で培った技術を使って目的を小さなタスクに分解し、情報収集や分析、成果物の作成までを自律的に進めるほか、ユーザーは途中で進捗を確認したり方針を変更したりでき、重要な操作の前には承認を求める。 ユーザーとプロンプトを交わしながら回答を返す従来の「チャット」とは異なり、達成したい目的を伝えるだけで、必要な作業を自ら分解し、実行まで担う ※クリックすると拡大画像が見られます 外部サービスとの連携窓口として、プラグインを集約した「Unified Plugins Directory」も新設した。Google Drive、SharePoint、Slack、Microsoft Teams、Gmail、Outlook、Salesforce、Adobe、Zoom、LinkedIn、GitHub、Canva、Dropboxなどのサービスと接続できる。「@」に続けてアプリ名を入力すれば使用するサービスを指定でき、指定しない場合はChatGPTが依頼内容に応じて参照すべきデータソースを判断する。 あわせて、ウェブサイトやウェブアプリを生成する「Sites」機能をパブリックベータとして公開した。手元の資料や接続した業務データをもとに、社内ポータル、ダッシュボード、プロジェクト管理表、公開用のインタラクティブレポートなどを作成し、URLで共有できる。情報源が更新された際に、作成したサイトの内容を更新することも可能だ。 Codexアプリを新ChatGPTアプリに刷新 MacとWindowsでは、ChatGPT Workに対応する新しいデスクトップ版ChatGPTを同日から世界で公開した。デスクトップ版では無料プランを含む全プランで、通常の「Chat」、一般業務向けの「Work」、ソフトウェア開発向けの「Codex」を切り替えて利用できる。ローカルファイルやパソコン上のアプリを操作できるほか、ウェブサイトやオンラインツールを扱う内蔵ブラウザも備える。 従来のCodexアプリは、新しいChatGPTデスクトップアプリに統合された。既存のChatGPTデスクトップアプリは「ChatGPT Classic」に改称され、当面は併存する。WorkはCodexと同じ利用体系を採用し、タスクの規模や複雑さ、使用するモデルによって利用枠の消費量が変わる。 ベータ期間中はNVIDIA、Zapier、RingCentral、ヴァージン・アトランティック航空などが試用した。Zapierでは毎月数千件に及ぶ営業リードの精査、NVIDIAではイベント準備や会議記録の分析、ヴァージン・アトランティック航空では競合他社との顧客体験の比較などに利用されたという。 Amazonで現在開催中のセールを見る Amazonのアソシエイトとして、CNET Japanは適格販売により収入を得ています

Web3・AI専門メディア 2026年7月13日 (更新: 2026年7月14日) 目次 米OpenAIは業務向けAIエージェント「ChatGPT Work」を発表した。複数のアプリやファイルから情報を集め、資料作成や分析、定期更新まで担う。ChatGPTを回答ツールから、実務を完遂する基盤へ進化させる動きだ。 ChatGPTが業務を分解し、数時間かけて完遂 2026年7月9日に公表されたChatGPT Workは、複雑な仕事を小さな工程に分け、必要に応じて数時間にわたり処理を続けるAIエージェントである。 SlackやMicrosoft Teams、Google Drive、メール、カレンダー、CRMなどと連携し、情報収集から分析、スライド、表計算、文書、Webアプリの作成までを一つの依頼で進められる。 基盤には同日発表のGPT-5.6を採用した。複数段階の推論や、テンプレート・参照資料に沿った成果物の生成能力を強化しており、月末の予算差異分析、営業会議の準備、顧客調査からキャンペーン素材への展開といった業務を想定する。 ユーザーは進捗を確認し、途中で方向を変えたり、重要な操作を承認したりできる。 さらに、スケジュール済みタスクを使えば、定例会議の資料更新や顧客フィードバックの監視などを継続的に実行可能だ。 デスクトップ版ではローカルファイルやアプリ、内蔵ブラウザを扱え、Codexも新しいChatGPTアプリへ統合された。 生産性向上の一方、権限管理が導入の焦点に 企業にとって最大の利点は、分断されていた業務を一つの文脈でつなげられる点にある。OpenAIの社内事例では、財務部門の月末締めと予測作業を数日から数時間へ短縮したという。 営業、マーケティング、分析、開発などで定型作業を委ねれば、人は判断や顧客対応に時間を振り向けやすくなる。 一方、接続する情報源が増えるほど、誤操作や機密情報の流出、誤った分析が連鎖するリスクも高まる。OpenAIはEnterpriseとEdu向けに、利用者、参照データ、接続ツール、実行可能な操作を管理する仕組みを用意するが、企業側にも承認フローや監査体制の整備が求められる。 Web・モバイル版はPro、Enterprise、Eduから順次提供され、PlusとBusinessにも数日以内に拡大する予定だ。新デスクトップアプリではFreeを含む全プランでChat、Work、Codexを利用できる。 今後は、AIの評価軸が回答精度だけでなく、業務を安全に完遂できるかへ移ると考えられる。 OpenAI公式発表 関連記事: MetaがMuse Spark 1.1を公開 records.title: AEOサービス「Answer IO」がOpenAIの最新モデル「GPT-5.6」に対応、3階層モデル（Sol・Terra・Luna）で階層別のブランド可視性測定を実現
records.excerpt: AEOサービス「Answer IO」がOpenAIの最新モデル「GPT-5.6」に対応、3階層モデル（Sol・Terra・Luna）で階層別のブランド可視性測定を実現 同じ「ChatGPT」でも応答モデルが変わる時代に、自社ブランドの見え方を階層別に測定 株式会社フィードフォース 2026年7月15日 11時00分 株式会社フィードフォース(本社:東京都港区、代表取締役社長:塚田 耕司、以下「フィードフォース」)は、AI検索におけるブランドの見え方を可視化する「Answer IO」で、OpenAI社が2026年7月9日に一般提供を開始した最新モデル「GPT-5.6」の測定に対応しました。GPT-5.6はSol(フラッグシップ)・Terra(バランス)・Luna(高速・低コスト)の3階層で提供され、同じ「ChatGPT」でも利用するプランや用途によって応答するモデルが変わります。今回の対応により、企業は自社ブランドが各階層でどのように評価されるかを階層別に測定でき、最新のAI検索環境に合わせてブランド可視性を把握できるようになります。 詳細を見る 「同じChatGPTでも見え方が変わる」——GPT-5.6対応の背景 ChatGPTをはじめとする生成AIは、いまや商品比較や企業選定など、ビジネスの情報探索・意思決定に日常的に使われています。ユーザーがAIに質問したとき、その回答に自社ブランドがどう登場し、どう評価されるかは、認知や検討に直接影響します。そのChatGPTの中核をなすモデルが、2026年7月9日に最新世代の「GPT-5.6」へと更新されました(※1)。ユーザーが接触するAI回答が新世代に切り替わることで、ブランドの言及パターンや評価も変化しうる状況になっています。 GPT-5.6のもう一つの特徴は、単一モデルではなくSol・Terra・Lunaの3階層のモデルファミリーとして提供される点です。Solは最上位のフラッグシップ、Terraは性能とコストのバランス型、Lunaは最速・最安の選択肢という位置づけで、同じ「ChatGPT」でも利用するプランや用途(通常チャット / Work / Codex)によって応答するモデルが異なります(※1)。階層によって推論の深さや情報探索の精度が変わるため、同一のクエリでも、どの階層で聞くかによってブランドの言及有無や評価が変わりうるという新しい論点が生まれています。 records.excerpt: 広告プラットフォームでは、自己評価による測定は常態化している。つまり、広告を販売した後、その広告の成果について報告を行うだけで、その計算を検証する独立した監査機関は存在しないということだ。最高マーケティング責任者（CMO）たちは通常、この状況を変えるために何年も奮闘しなければならない。 DIGIDAY+ AI , PLATFORMS OpenAI 、上場に向けて不可欠な広告主の信頼と外部検証のロードマップ 編集部 2026/7/14 記事のポイント OpenAIは広告主の信頼獲得と上場を見据え、業界で常態化する「自前の効果測定」を排し、サードパーティによる透明な測定基準の導入を進めている。 ユーザーのプライバシー保護のためチャット内容を開示できない同社にとって、広告効果を証明しメディア予算を確保するには外部検証が不可欠となる。 外部での測定は不正を防ぐが、従来の検索広告とは異なる「対話型AI独自の広告フォーマットや影響力の測定手法」の確立という本質的課題への対応は今なお模索中だ。 広告プラットフォームでは、自己評価による測定は常態化している。つまり、広告を販売した後、その広告の成果について報告を行うだけで、その計算を検証する独立した監査機関は存在しないということだ。最高マーケティング責任者（CMO）たちは通常、この状況を変えるために何年も奮闘しなければならない。しかし、OpenAIは待つことなく行動を起こすことにした。 OpenAIの広告部門責任者であるデイビッド・デュガン氏は、米DIGIDAYの取材に対し、サードパーティによる測定の導入は、同プラットフォームの現状からすれば「自然な進化」だと語った。現在、広告主が入手できるのは入札データと成果データのみだ。そのいずれからも、広告が実在する人物に届いたことを証明することはできない。さらに言えば、これはOpenAIが自らの成果を自己評価しているに過ぎない。サードパーティによる測定が行われれば状況は一変し、広告が実際の人間によって、視認可能な状態で、かつブランドに安全な環境で閲覧されたことが確認されることになる。もっとも、それも「ある程度まで」の話だ。検証ベンダーにも、手法をめぐる論争や見落としがあるという過去の歴史があるからだ。デュガン氏は、マーケターがいつ検証を行えるようになるかについては明言を避けたが、どこと組むかについてはヒントを示した。 「我々が発展していくなかでは当然、どのような信頼できるサードパーティパートナーと提携し、連携を図っていくべきかについて検討していくことになる」とデュガン氏は話す。「現時点で具体的な社名を伝えることはできないが、信頼できる業界パートナーと協力することは、広告主やエージェンシー、そしてパートナー各社からしばしば期待される自然な流れであり、我々もその点を尊重している」。 ［▼会員登録をして続きを読む▼］ Advertisement 「我々が発展していくなかでは当然、どのような信頼できるサードパーティパートナーと提携し、連携を図っていくべきかについて検討していくことになる」とデュガン氏は話す。「現時点で具体的な社名を伝えることはできないが、信頼できる業界パートナーと協力することは、広告主やエージェンシー、そしてパートナー各社からしばしば期待される自然な流れであり、我々もその点を尊重している」。 広告事業の立ち上げと検索とは異なる測定へのアプローチ その率直な発言は、計画がそう遠くはない将来に実現しそうなことを示唆しており、それは驚くことではない。OpenAIの広告事業は、他社の多くよりも早く軌道に乗っているからだ。わずか4カ月で、（現時点で） 7つの市場 でのサービスを開始し、広告担当幹部を採用し、商業パートナーシップを締結し、 測定ツール を作り上げ、 広告マネージャー を立ち上げてみせたのだ。Googleやメタ（Meta）といった企業が同じことを実現するには、数年とは言わないまでも、これより長い時間がかかった。 「だからこそ、ロードマップを検討するにあたっては、広告主からの期待がどのようなものかを確実に考慮し、それをどのように実現できるかを考えていく」とドュガン氏は話す。「これは（ユーザーにとって）まったく新しい体験であり、一部の指標をどのように進化させていくかを検討する必要があると思う。業界はどのように進化すべきか、また、検索などほかのチャネルとは異なる視点で考える必要があるだろう」。 これは重要なポイントだ。その理由は、OpenAIが直面するより根本的な課題のひとつに直結していることにある──これは検索ではない。そのため、従来のパフォーマンス測定手法をそのまま適用することはできないのだ。 デュガン氏はこの点についてさらに詳しく話した。「この業界はどのように進化すべきか、そして検索などほかのチャネルとは異なる視点で考える必要があるのか。そのためのプレイブックはこれまでとは異なるものになるはずなので、我々とこれらのパートナー企業とのあいだには、非常に興味深い協業が生まれると思う」。 上場を見据えた外部検証の必要性とチャットボット広告の根本的課題 すべてはそのプレイブックの出来具合にかかっている。OpenAIが上場することになれば──同社はすでに米証券取引委員会（SEC）にS-1フォーム（米国企業が新規株式公開[IPO]を行う際、SECへ提出が義務付けられている「証券登録届出書」兼「目論見書」）を 秘密裏に提出済み records.excerpt: OpenAI's new flagship model deletes files on its own, people keep warning | TechCrunch TechCrunch Desktop Logo TechCrunch Mobile Logo Topics Latest AI Amazon Apps Biotech & Health Climate Cloud Computing Commerce Crypto Enterprise EVs Fintech Fundraising Gadgets Gaming Google Government & Policy Hardware Instagram Layoffs Media & Entertainment Meta Microsoft Privacy Robotics Security Social Space Startups TikTok Transportation Venture More from TechCrunch Staff Events Startup Battlefield StrictlyVC Newsletters Podcasts Videos Partner Content TechCrunch Brand Studio Crunchboard Contact Us Image Credits: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images AI OpenAI’s new flagship model deletes files on its own, people keep warning Julie Bort 2:50 PM PDT · July 14, 2026 Users of OpenAI’s latest coding and cybersecurity-oriented flagship model, GPT-5.6 Sol, are posting horrifying accounts on social media, claiming the model just up and deleted their files, data, even entire databases on its own, without asking first. “GPT-5.6-Sol just accidentally deleted almost ALL of my Mac’s files,” wrote Matt Shumer, the founder and CEO of AI startup OthersideAI, maker of HyperWrite, in a now viral post on X . “GPT-5.6 Sol just deleted my whole production database. That’s it. Not a joke. This had never happened to me before, with any other model, ever,” developer Bruno Lemos posted on X . “Looks like I’ve gotten bit by Codex Sol’s overly ambitious system and it deleted some files it shouldn’t have. I have backups so I’ll be fine, but this is not cool, Sol needs to be toned down,” posted developer Joey Kudish. A Reddit post has collected more examples. True, a handful of users making such claims — even one as credible as Shumer — isn’t statistically reliable evidence that the model is solely at fault. Plenty of other variables can cause an AI system to misbehave. But OpenAI itself flagged this risk before Sol ever shipped. Two weeks before OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Sol, the company published a system card for the model — the paper that documents model-testing methods and results. Naturally, the system card largely extols the capabilities of Sol, as these reports typically do. But it also includes a warning of sorts (bold emphasis ours): In coding contexts, misalignment generally stems from a mix of overeagerness to complete the task and interpreting user instructions too permissively — assuming that actions are allowed unless they’re explicitly and unambiguously prohibited. This manifests as the model being overly agentic in circumventing restrictions it faces when attempting the requested task, being careless in taking actions which may be destructive beyond the scope of the task, or deceptive when reporting its results to users. In other words, OpenAI found that Sol has a tendency to take whatever actions it thinks gets a job done, even destructive ones, as long as those actions aren’t “unambiguously” prohibited. Then it might lie about what caused it to do so. OpenAI shared examples. In one case, the user told Sol to delete three remote virtual machines (cloud-based computers), named 1, 2, and 3. But Sol couldn’t find those names in the place where it looked, so instead of stopping to ask, it decided to delete three other virtual machines, 5, 6, and 7, the paper notes. In doing so, it “killed active processes, and force-removed worktrees [the working files tied to a coding project]. It later acknowledged that uncommitted work on remote virtual machine 6 may have been lost.” In short, it deleted the wrong machines, on its own, and only admitted what it did after the fact. In another instance, Sol “used credentials beyond what the user had authorized.” Credentials are the usernames, passwords, or security keys a system uses to verify who’s allowed to log in. This incident occurred when Sol was working on a project and couldn’t read its cloud files. Rather than alerting the user to the problem, Sol went looking for the credentials on its own, found some sitting in a hidden local cache, and then used them without asking for authorization from the user. The system card does promise that destructive behavior should be rare, although it also admits that GPT-5.6 Sol “shows a greater tendency than GPT-5.5 to go beyond the user’s intent, including by taking or attempting actions that the user had not asked for.” It’s too soon to say how widespread these incidents — Sol deleting files, or sifting out credentials the user didn’t give it — really are. In the meantime, Sol users should be prepared to implement their own safeguards with the model, like using permission scoping (that doesn’t give access to production systems), maintaining backups, and staging rollouts. records.excerpt: Apple's OpenAI lawsuit signals a new AI battleground: Talent IT Staffing & Careers IT Strategy Machine Learning & AI News Apple's OpenAI lawsuit signals a new AI battleground: Talent The alleged theft of trade secrets points to institutional knowledge and employee expertise as the new competitive differentiator in the AI race. July 14, 2026 6 Min Read Getty Images Apple has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and several former Apple employees, alleging trade-secret theft of unreleased Apple products. The accusation is tied to OpenAI's ambitions to develop AI-integrated hardware; according to Reuters , Apple claims its rival has pursued a "broad effort to systematically acquire and exploit Apple's ‌confidential information through former employees, recruiting practices and supplier relationships." OpenAI has denied the allegations. The lawsuit will ultimately be decided in court, but it arrives at a moment when the AI industry is wrestling with a broader question about where competitive advantage truly lies. For much of the generative AI boom, the race was defined by access. Companies competed for GPUs, data center capacity and the most capable models. Those advantages still matter, but they are no longer the only ones that matter. As frontier AI becomes more widely available, the conversation is shifting from who can access the technology to who can apply it most effectively. And that increasingly comes down to employee skill sets and institutional knowledge. Related: 2026 tech company layoffs "Institutional knowledge isn't just people, it's the data and processes they control," said Sam Caucci, CEO and founder of 1Huddle, a workforce coaching and development platform. "When your best people leave, they take proprietary data sets, training methodologies and competitive context." As AI becomes embedded in products, business processes and decision-making, organizations are increasingly being forced to think about the governance of knowledge itself. "This case reflects a broader question emerging in AI competition: Where do we draw the line between an individual's expertise and an organization's proprietary knowledge?" said Zakaria Laaraj, founder of Global New Ventures, an educational digital consultancy. "In that sense, AI competition is becoming as much a human challenge as a technological one." Beyond the AI model race The assumption that better models automatically create sustainable advantage is becoming harder to defend. Organizations can increasingly access similar frontier capabilities through cloud providers, APIs and commercial platforms. As AI accessibility and adoption becomes more ubiquitous, the competitive advantage of AI is underscored more by enterprises' ability to use the technology to deliver ROI and business outcomes. "The next phase of AI competition will not be defined solely by organizations that have access to the best-performing models," Laaraj said. "It will be defined by organizations that are able to effectively develop, retain and translate human expertise into organizational capability." Related: Bridging the gap between leadership's AI enthusiasm and employee pushback Kyle Elliott, a career and executive coach who works with technology leaders, made a similar point from a commercial perspective: "Building an advanced AI model is no longer enough to attract customers or generate a profit. Companies also need people who know how to transform those models into products that drive revenue and, ultimately, returns for shareholders." That distinction helps explain why the movement of employees has become such a sensitive issue. A company can license a model and buy compute. What is much harder to acquire is the accumulated experience that comes from building products, understanding customers and navigating the operational realities of bringing technology to market. "Much of that advantage comes from experience that isn't written down anywhere," Elliott said. "You can't merely download that experience from a model. You either develop it internally or hire for it." The new competitive moat If models are becoming more accessible, what becomes the defensible advantage? Caucci said he believes the answer lies at the heart of the organization. "The real competitive moat [is] control of data, inputs and institutional knowledge," he said. "Frontier models are becoming commodities, but your proprietary data sets and how you train on them aren't." Related: The leadership desert: The unspoken enterprise IT talent problem The technology itself may be increasingly available, but every organization possesses a unique combination of data, processes, relationships and expertise that competitors cannot easily replicate. Laaraj similarly argued that organizations often misunderstand where the most valuable knowledge actually resides: "Beyond documentation and intellectual property, it is reflected in how people collaborate, make decisions, solve problems and share expertise across teams." For Caucci, that means institutional knowledge deserves to be treated as a strategic asset — and employee retention needs to be a priority . "Constant turnover destroys that advantage because you lose both the talent and the institutional knowledge of how to use your data to make strategic decisions," he said. That creates a challenge for enterprises that are simultaneously trying to recruit AI talent in a competitive field, retain existing employees and protect what makes them distinctive. The goal, Laaraj argued, should not be to prevent knowledge from moving; an element of that is unavoidable in today's labor market. Instead, organizations should focus on ensuring that critical expertise becomes embedded throughout the business rather than concentrated in a handful of individuals. "The real differentiator is not individual expertise alone, but the ability to transform that expertise into organizational capability," he said. Why governance matters more than ever The Apple lawsuit is unlikely to be the last dispute of its kind. As organizations invest more heavily in AI talent, experts expect questions around intellectual property, employee mobility and knowledge ownership to become increasingly common. Elliott expects these tensions to be exacerbated by the demand for experienced AI professionals , which continues to outpace supply. "The pool of truly experienced AI talent is slim, and the compensation packages are climbing," he said. "When companies shell out millions in total compensation for individual hires, part of what they're paying for is what's in that person's head." That expensive reality places new pressure on governance practices that have often been treated as secondary concerns. Elliott pointed to offboarding as one example: Organizations frequently devote substantial resources to recruiting and onboarding employees, while paying far less attention to how they leave. He argued offboarding should be considered as important as onboarding — "if not more so." "One CIO at a multibillion-dollar company recently shared with me that he is leading a global project to track down the more than 40 systems where hundreds of terminated contractors still had access to critical company data. All of that risk was avoidable with a proper offboarding process," he said. Elliott also emphasized the importance of documentation, particularly among senior leaders and technical specialists: "If your product roadmap or pricing strategy only lives in someone's head, it walks out the door with them." Building a sustainable talent strategy As AI capabilities spread across the market, enterprises are increasingly competing on something more difficult to purchase outright: talent. records.excerpt: Title: OpenAI to join the smart speaker party: Following Amazon, Google, and Apple into the AI companion era URL Source: http://news.google.?oc=5 Published Time: 2026-07-14T21:58:17+00:00 Markdown Content: [![Image 1: Apple's HomePod](https://i0.wp.com/macdailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/homepod-select-202210_FMT_WHH.jpeg?resize=640%2C600&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/macdailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/homepod-select-202210_FMT_WHH.jpeg?ssl=1) [Apple’s](http://news.google.?oc=5#) HomePod OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, the AI for newbies who don’t know better alternatives exist, is stepping into consumer hardware with its first device: a movable, screen-free smart speaker designed as an always-on AI companion for the home. According to a [_Bloomberg News_ report](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-14/openai-s-first-device-will-be-moveable-screenless-speaker-built-as-ai-companion), the product — still in development — aims to control smart-home devices, play media, answer questions, handle messages, and leverage ChatGPT’s capabilities. This sounds innovative on paper, especially with the promise of a more “humanlike” AI presence. But let’s be clear: Amazon, Google, and [Apple](http://news.google.?oc=5#) pioneered this category years ago. OpenAI isn’t breaking new ground here — it’s trying to catch up to a market these giants have dominated for nearly a decade. Company News [![Image 2: In addition to midnight, HomePod mini is available in yellow, orange, blue, and white.](https://i0.wp.com/macdailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/240715_homepod_mini_02.png?resize=640%2C640&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/macdailynews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/240715_homepod_mini_02.png?ssl=1) Apple’s HomePod mini **The Smart Speaker Revolution Started Long Before ChatGPT** Amazon lit the fuse in 2014 with the original Echo and Alexa. What began as a cylindrical speaker that could play music, set timers, and answer basic questions quickly evolved into a full ecosystem. Echo devices now control lights, thermostats, door locks, and more — exactly the smart-home hub role OpenAI envisions. Amazon iterated relentlessly with cheaper Dots, portable versions, and premium models, shipping hundreds of millions of units and embedding Alexa into countless third-party devices. Google followed in 2016 with Google Home (later Nest Audio and similar), emphasizing superior search integration and natural language understanding powered by its vast data resources. These speakers became central to many households for information, entertainment, and automation. Apple entered the fray in 2018 with the HomePod, focusing on premium audio quality and tight integration with its ecosystem, later adding the more affordable HomePod mini. By the time OpenAI is targeting a potential 2027 launch for its device, smart speakers will have been mainstream for over a dozen years. The core features OpenAI highlights — voice interaction, media playback, smart-home control, and AI assistance — are table stakes that consumers already expect. **What’s New (or Not So New) with OpenAI’s Approach?** Discover more phones Manufacturing TV & Video Equipment The _Bloomberg News_ description by Mark Gurman positions OpenAI’s speaker as a “new type of home computer for the AI era,” movable and screen-free for ambient use. Earlier reports suggest possible camera integration for environmental awareness, object recognition, and even facial recognition for purchases — features that echo (pun intended) what existing devices already offer or are evolving toward. Many current smart speakers and displays already include cameras, microphones that listen continuously (with privacy toggles), and advanced AI for proactive suggestions. OpenAI’s edge is presumably its cutting-edge language models, potentially enabling more conversational, context-aware interactions than today’s assistants. Yet even here, competitors aren’t standing still: Google has integrated Gemini, Amazon continues enhancing Alexa with generative AI, and Apple is finally significantly deepening Siri with on-device intelligence in its ecosystem. Company News **Privacy Concerns Loom Large, Especially Versus Apple** One area where OpenAI’s entry raises fresh questions is privacy. An always-listening, camera-equipped AI companion that processes conversations, surroundings, and potentially personal interactions could amass intimate data about users’ daily lives. OpenAI has faced broader scrutiny over how it handles training data and user inputs with its models, and a device that lives in the home would amplify those risks — including potential data sharing, advertising uses, or breaches. In contrast, Apple has long positioned itself as a privacy leader in the smart speaker space. HomePod devices prioritize on-device processing where possible, use randomized identifiers instead of linking data to user accounts, and offer straightforward controls to delete Siri history. Apple’s ecosystem design generally minimizes cloud transmission and avoids using customer data for ad targeting in the same way its competitors do. OpenAI, as a newer hardware player heavily reliant on cloud-based AI, will need to earn similar trust — something that could prove challenging given the always-on nature of the proposed companion. **Challenges Ahead for the Newcomer** Discover more Apple news summaries phone Apple iPhone OpenAI enters a crowded, mature market where hardware margins are thin, privacy concerns run high, and user loyalty to existing ecosystems (Amazon for shopping, Google for search, Apple for seamless device handoff) is strong. Building reliable hardware at scale, managing always-listening microphones and potential cameras responsibly, and competing on price (rumored $200–$300 range) won’t be trivial. History shows that smart speakers succeeded because they solved simple, everyday problems affordably and reliably — not because they promised revolutionary AI companionship. OpenAI’s version may feel more “alive” thanks to advanced models, but it risks being perceived as a me-too product unless it delivers truly standout experiences that justify switching or adding yet another device to the home. ‎ **MacDail

Vincee Cole Jul 14 5 mins read Sponsored X LinkedIn Email Facebook Copy link TL;DR Apple alleges OpenAI systematically recruited employees to extract hardware trade secrets Two former Apple employees, Tang Tan and Chang Liu, are named as defendants The lawsuit could delay OpenAI's AI hardware device and upcoming IPO Apple has already replaced OpenAI with Google Gemini for its rebuilt Siri Apple's complaint is the most detailed public account of OpenAI's secret hardware program Apple filed a federal lawsuit against OpenAI on July 10, accusing the AI company of systematically stealing trade secrets to build a competing consumer hardware device. The complaint, filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, names OpenAI, two former Apple employees, and Jony Ive’s hardware startup io Products as defendants. The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI’s hardware division was built on stolen Apple intellectual property, with the company’s chief hardware officer using job interviews as intelligence-gathering sessions and coaching departing employees on how to bypass Apple’s security protocols. Apple described the alleged operation as happening “at every level” of OpenAI’s organization. What the Apple OpenAI Lawsuit Alleges Apple’s complaint centers on two former employees who now hold key positions at OpenAI. Tang Tan spent 24 years at Apple and rose to vice president of product design for the iPhone and Apple Watch. He left the company in early 2024 to co-found io Products with former Apple chief design officer Jony Ive. OpenAI acquired io Products in May 2025 for approximately $6.5 billion , and Tan became OpenAI’s chief hardware officer. According to the filing, Tan allegedly used confidential Apple project codenames during interviews with current Apple employees, directed job candidates to bring physical Apple components to “show and tell” sessions at OpenAI, and circulated an internal Apple offboarding document to help departing employees avoid security checks. Recruits were also asked to prepare “Technical Deep Dive” presentations about unreleased Apple products. Chang Liu , a senior systems electrical engineer who spent eight years at Apple, left for OpenAI in January 2026 . Apple alleges that Liu failed to return a company laptop, discovered a bug that gave him continued access to Apple’s cloud file storage, and downloaded dozens of confidential hardware files while already working at OpenAI. According to Axios , Liu celebrated the security flaw in a message to a former Apple colleague. That colleague, Alyssa Peng, allegedly helped retrieve additional files through her own work laptop before eventually joining OpenAI herself. Apple also accused OpenAI of approaching Apple’s manufacturing partners with confidential information. In one instance, OpenAI allegedly convinced a trusted supplier to demonstrate a proprietary metal-finishing technique, misleading the partner into believing Apple had given permission. From WWDC Partners to Federal Court The speed of this relationship’s collapse is striking. Apple and OpenAI announced their partnership at WWDC in June 2024 , with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appearing alongside Apple executives to unveil ChatGPT’s integration into iOS, iPadOS, and macOS. The deal looked like a natural fit. Apple needed to close its AI gap after falling behind ChatGPT and Google Gemini. OpenAI wanted access to more than a billion iPhone users to drive ChatGPT Plus subscriptions. The relationship started deteriorating less than a year later. OpenAI’s $6.5 billion acquisition of io Products in May 2025 signaled that the AI company intended to compete directly with Apple in consumer hardware. By December 2025, dozens of Apple employees had migrated to OpenAI , including engineers and designers with experience in audio, watch design, and robotics. In early 2026, the situation escalated on multiple fronts. Apple announced in January that it was replacing OpenAI with Google Gemini as the foundation for its rebuilt Siri in iOS 27 , paying Google roughly $1 billion per year for a custom 1.2 trillion parameter model. In April, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo reported that OpenAI was developing a smartphone built around AI agents rather than apps. As Memeburn reported in May , OpenAI was already considering its own legal action against Apple, alleging that Apple had failed to adequately promote ChatGPT within iOS. Apple sent OpenAI a letter in February raising concerns about potential trade secret theft. According to the court filing, OpenAI never responded. Five months later, Apple sued. The 400-Employee Number Needs Context The number 400 is the figure Apple leads with in the complaint, and it is worth examining carefully. Apple says more than 400 of its former employees now work at OpenAI. That figure alone does not prove wrongdoing. Apple employs well over 100,000 people, and employees leave large companies routinely. California does not enforce noncompete agreements, which is why trade secrets law is the only legal mechanism Apple has to control what former employees carry with them. But Apple is using the number to establish a pattern. The company argues that OpenAI’s recruitment process was structured to extract confidential information during interviews, and that departing employees were coached on avoiding Apple’s standard offboarding procedures. If Apple can demonstrate in discovery that even a fraction of those 400 brought protected material, the aggregate exposure becomes significant. Most of the recruiting targeted Apple’s hardware engineering division, the group led by John Ternus , who is set to become Apple’s CEO in September 2026. Ternus and Tang Tan once competed for the top hardware role at Apple. This suggests the lawsuit carries a personal dimension beyond corporate strategy, and it will be among the first major legal battles Ternus oversees as incoming chief executive. What the Lawsuit Reveals About OpenAI’s Secret Device A less discussed implication of this filing is what Apple chose to make public. Trade secret lawsuits typically involve confidentiality orders and sealed filings, because the plaintiff risks exposing the very information it wants to protect. Apple’s complaint went in the opposite direction. It described System-in-Package modules, proprietary metal-finishing processes, supply chain relationships, and specific engineering workflows that OpenAI allegedly targeted. Forbes reported that the complaint amounts to the most detailed public account of OpenAI’s secret hardware program that has surfaced from any source. This may indicate that Apple made a deliberate calculation. By detailing what OpenAI allegedly took, Apple accomplishes two things simultaneously. It strengthens its legal claim by showing specificity rather than vague allegations. records.title: OpenAI's Ad Business Is on Pace to Miss Its Own Forecast By 90%, Analyst Says
records.excerpt: OpenAI is projecting $100 billion in ad revenue by 2030. Emarketer puts the ceiling for the entire chatbot ad market at just $5.41 billion. OpenAI’s ad business is on pace to fall short of the company’s own five-year revenue forecast by 90%, according to Emarketer. The AI lab has projected $2.5 billion in ad revenue this year and $100 billion by 2030. Emarketer’s data finds that standalone chatbots like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot app, Google AI Mode, and Amazon Alexa for Shopping (formerly Rufus) in U.S, will generate less than $1 billion in ad revenue this year, and just $5.41 billion by 2030. OpenAI began its ad trial in February. Two months in, the AI lab made headlines touting those same projections. The forecast assumes OpenAI captures search ad budgets en masse from traditional search ad sellers, dominates a fully mature chatbot ad market, and outperforms every ad format in history--all at once. “If you're willing to accept all those assumptions, then I can see their reported forecasts being true,” said Nate Elliot, principal analyst, AI, Emarketer. “But we're not willing to accept any of those assumptions.” Ad spend inside AI assistants like ChatGPT will account for just 8% of the total digital ad spend this year, according to Emarketer data. Total digital ad spend will reach $32.03 billion in 2026, more than doubling to $68.25 billion in 2030. Most of that AI-linked spend is barely going to chatbots at all. More than 80% of AI advertising in 2026 will appear next to AI content, like traditional search ads running alongside Google’s AI Overviews, generating $26.42 billion in the U.S this year alone. Even as growth slows, that category will still represent 58.6% of AI ad spending in 2030. “Even if you assume that they will make 100% of all revenue from chatbot advertising five years from now, OpenAI will still miss their number by 90%,” Elliot said. Hitting that target requires growth across three separate variables at once, according Matt Prohaska, ceo and principal of Prohaska Consulting: total audience size, average revenue per user, and the ad products themselves. OpenAI's recent push to court small businesses is one attempt to grow some of that pie. But "it's not like small business ad spend is going to be up 25% a year," Prohaska said. "That TAM is a little more limited." The dizzying numbers come ahead of the much anticipated IPO which the company filed last month. “If you look at the total addressable market OpenAI has put in their filings—the trillions they think they're going to be taking from other places or creating—obviously they have to throw a number that's huge to justify a trillion-dollar valuation for an IPO that is smartly being delayed right now,” Prohaska said. OpenAI did not respond to media request. How OpenAI built its ad business in five months The ChatGPT ad pilot formally began on February 9 this year, launching in the U.S with a minimum spend commitment as high as $250,000. By March, OpenAI began testing an ads manager with a small group of advertisers. In comparison, it took Netflix about two years to launch a self-serve platform after starting its ad business, and Meta about three years. That pilot crossed the $100 million annualized revenue mark within six weeks of launch–the same day OpenAI announced expansion to Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. At the same time, the company named David Dugan, a longtime ad executive at Meta, as its vp and head of global ads solutions. By April, OpenAI quietly dropped its minimum spend threshold to $50,000, ADWEEK previously reported, widening the funnel to tap a broader pool of advertisers. According to Kevin Roy, founder of GreenBanana SEO, who has been testing ads on ChatGPT since June for his own company as well for fewer than a dozen clients, the highest anyone is spending is $5,000. OpenAI is also inching towards a more sophisticated ad product. According to Juozas Kaziukėnas, advisor at ecommerce ad platform Quartile, the company is rolling out conversion-optimized ads, or oCPC on ads manager. Kaziukėnas first saw the support for this infrastructure roughly a month ago, and as recently as last week, an update to the UI that supports it. This new capability allows advertisers to adjust bids real-time based on the predicted likelihood that a given click will convert into sale. “If you are an ecommerce store, you are buying ads to drive sales. The smarter conversion optimized ad strategy works better for you because OpenAI’s ad platform is optimizing for the outcome you want,” Kaziukėnas said. That builds on click and conversion metrics OpenAi has already rolled out--laying the groundwork to turn ChatGPT into a full performance-advertising engine. OpenAI also inked deals across Madison Avenue, allowing advertisers to buy ads via Criteo, StackAdapt, and LiveRamp. By May, OpenAI said it would expand its ad pilot to more countries, including U.K, Japan, Brazil, among others. “They're not running an ad trial by any discernible metric,” said Elliot. “In an ad trial, you'd be running a small number of these ads to a small number of users, and you would have more leeway to experiment and try new ideas.” Growth is slowing just as OpenAI leans on it ChatGPT reached 1 billion global app monthly active users in May 2026, according to Sensor Tower estimates, up 63% year-over-year. This comes on the heels of OpenAI touting 900 MAU and 50 million consumer subscribers, as of February. But the growth curve is bending. ChatGPT’s app MAU grew 140% YoY in the first quarter of 2026, sharply down from 362% YoY in the same quarter a year ago. Still, ChatGPT remains larger than rivals like Claude (59 million), and Gemini (484 million MAUs), per Sensor Tower data. But the deceleration undercuts a key assumption in OpenAI’s ad forecast: that user growth keeps compounding fast enough to support a rapidly scaling ad business. Ads run only on Free and Go tier accounts--meaning the platform’s heaviest users don't see them at all, Elliot noted. “By definition, the most active users--the people who spend the most time submit the most prompts--won't see ads,” he said. “There are Token limits for usage. If you aren't paying for subs, you aren't using it everyday.” Sources interviewed for this story said advertisers are treating ChatGPT ads as an experiment budget and not sweating for any meaningful ROI. Roy said OpenAI still has a long way to go: build out audience data, negative keyword options, transparent triggering reports like those provided by Google ads. “The way that the ChatGPT interface is right now, is it ever going to be as sexy as a Meta ad or Google or PMax?,” Roy said. “Probably not.”

records.title: OpenAI’s latest model appears to delete users’ data without permission
records.excerpt: The latest version of OpenAI’s coding tool, GPT 5.6 Sol, has been accused of deleting important data without permission when allowed to operate autonomously. OpenAI’s latest model appears to delete users’ data without permission By Isaac Hanson 14/07/2026 The latest version of OpenAI’s coding tool, GPT-5.6 Sol, has been accused of deleting important data without permission when allowed to operate autonomously. When the model released to the public on Thursday , the artificial intelligence giant said Sol “sets a new standard for both intelligence and efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art results across coding, knowledge work, cybersecurity, and science while outperforming previous and competing frontier models with fewer tokens and at lower estimated cost.” Now, reports are coming in from multiple large accounts on social media platform X that the software is not always acting as intended. Matt Schumer, a tech investor and former AI company chief executive with over 370,000 followers, posted on Friday that Sol “just accidentally deleted almost ALL of my Mac’s files,” after a subagent’s cleanup command accidentally targeted his entire user folder. Schumer said in reply to comments that this was a “super freak accident”, but he does not appear to be the only one running into issues. BridgeMind, an AI startup with over 45,000 followers on X, posted Monday that code written by the Sol model cancelled every standing subscription by clients made through Stripe. The company claimed that this cost it thousands in monthly recurring revenue, and occurred while the owner slept. A third user, Sterling Crispin, a software developer with nearly 45,000 followers, posted that he set GPT-5.6 Sol to work towards a goal for two days, in which time it wrote 200,000 lines of code. When “gently questioned”, it reverted it all, saying 80 per cent of it was “a waste of time”. Sol is more error prone than previous models by OpenAI’s own admission, too. Despite remaining relatively low in real terms, documentation released by the company for its GPT-5.6 Sol model shows that it is around 10 times more likely to circumvent reasonable user restrictions than its predecessor GPT-5.5. Mistakes, known as “misalignment” in AI parlance, included claiming to have completed work it had not, unauthorised deletion of files on virtual machines and using credentials beyond what it had been authorised to use. NTN has approached OpenAI for comment on the matter. Share Story:

records.title: Wider ChatGPT Search access cuts traditional search 9.4%, study finds
records.excerpt: A 45,386-household clickstream panel found ChatGPT clicks out on 5.2% of sessions, Google 31.1%. Wider access cut traditional search 17% within twenty weeks. Wider ChatGPT Search access cuts traditional search 9.4%, study finds by Luis Rijo Luis Rijo Luís Rijo is a seasoned marketing professional with over 10 years of experience in Digital Marketing, Search, Social, Display, Video, and DOOH. Based in Europe. Also writing in the spend. Reach out via luis@ppc.land LinkedIn • July 13, 2026 • 10 min read Share on X Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on Pinterest Email Cobalt funnel absorbs a flood of search queries, releasing only a thin red trickle out the spout. A study published July 8, 2026 by researchers at Bocconi University found that expanding access to ChatGPT Search reduced traditional search engine queries by 9.4% on average, with the decline deepening to 17.0% after twenty weeks of exposure, based on desktop clickstream data covering more than 45,000 United States households. According to the paper, titled "Answering Without Referring: How AI Search Rewrites the Web's Economic Bargain," the authors are Qiaoni Shi, Kai Zhu, and Kai Gu, and the work was posted to the arXiv preprint server under the Computers and Society category. The research draws on URL-level Comscore desktop clickstream records spanning October 2024 through July 2025, a window chosen because it captures the staggered rollout of ChatGPT Search to different tiers of OpenAI's user base. Rather than relying on survey responses or platform-reported figures, the authors reconstructed individual browsing sessions from raw page loads, HTTP referrers, and timestamps, then compared how often a ChatGPT conversation or a Google query ended with a visit to an outside website. A different kind of search denominator Much of the existing public commentary on AI search traffic has measured click-through rates against a results-page impression or a bounded browsing session. The Bocconi team instead anchored its measurement to what it calls an information-seeking occasion: one ChatGPT conversation session, treated as a single unit regardless of how many messages it contained, compared against one Google search query. Using that framing, the study found that ChatGPT produced a clean outbound referral in only 5.2% of conversation sessions, compared with 31.1% of Google queries pooled across the ten-month sample. The gap was even starker at the household level. Among the 56,578 households that used ChatGPT during the panel window, 74.4% never generated a single clean referral to an outside website across the entire ten months. For Google, the equivalent zero-referral share among 291,747 querying households was 9.6%. The researchers tested whether this gap could be explained by differences between the kinds of households that gravitate toward each platform, or by broader shifts happening across particular calendar weeks. Restricting the analysis to household-weeks in which the same household used both ChatGPT and Google, and adding fixed effects for household identity and calendar week, moved the estimated gap only marginally, from a raw 31.5 percentage-point difference to 29.0 points. The persistence of the gap under this stricter test indicates that the difference is not primarily driven by who uses each service, but by how each service behaves once a person is using it. Where the residual clicks go The clicks that did leave ChatGPT were not simply a smaller version of what Google sent out. When the authors classified destination websites by content type and monetization model, ChatGPT's referral pool showed a heavier concentration in reference and knowledge sites, developer and technical resources, academic research destinations, and general-purpose software tools, while showing markedly less traffic to social media platforms and to e-commerce marketplaces than Google's referral stream did over the same window. On monetization, the tilt was pronounced. ChatGPT's residual referrals favored nonprofit and public-interest websites, freemium software products, and subscription-supported destinations, while sending proportionally less traffic to advertising-supported websites than Google did. Because advertising-supported sites depend on routed visits to generate ad impressions, this composition detail carries direct implications for how publishers that rely on programmatic or direct-sold display inventory might experience the shift toward conversational search. The paper also examined how concentrated each platform's referral traffic was across destination websites. Measured in aggregate across the entire sample, Google's referral pool proved between 1.87 and 3.47 times more concentrated than ChatGPT's, depending on which cutoff was applied to the destination universe, with Google's clicks converging heavily on a small number of large platforms. Within an individual household's own week-to-week activity, however, that difference mostly disappeared. Among lightly active households, the concentration of ChatGPT referrals and Google referrals was statistically indistinguishable, and only among the heaviest-referring households did ChatGPT's traffic become more concentrated than Google's. The authors interpret this as evidence that ChatGPT's apparent diversity at the aggregate level is a pattern of different households reaching different niche destinations, rather than any single household spreading its own attention more evenly. The access-expansion test To move beyond correlation, the researchers exploited three dates on which OpenAI widened who could use ChatGPT Search. According to OpenAI's own rollout announcement, referenced in the paper, access opened to paid subscribers on October 31, 2024, to free logged-in users on December 16, 2024, and to users browsing without an account on February 5, 2025. Because these expansion dates were set by OpenAI's product rollout schedule rather than by any individual household's decision to adopt the feature, the authors argue the timing offers a cleaner test of cause and effect than simply comparing early adopters against everyone else. Pooling all three expansions and comparing newly eligible households against a control group with no prior ChatGPT or Claude activity, the study found that traditional search queries - covering Google, Bing, and Yahoo - fell by 3.14 queries per household per week immediately following expanded access, a 9.4% decline relative to the pre-expansion average of 33.51 weekly queries. That effect deepened as more time passed: by the twentieth week after access opened, the decline had grown to 17.0% of the pre-expansion baseline. A narrower comparison, restricted to the December 2024 expansion and pitting newly-eligible logged-in users against not-yet-eligible anonymous users who were already familiar with the ChatGPT interface, produced a smaller but directionally consistent decline of 8.2% after twenty weeks. The category breakdown of that displacement is where the paper's implications for publishers sharpen. Search-engine referral visits fell most steeply for academic research destinations, down 32.8%, followed by reference and knowledge sites at 26.5%, developer and technical resources at 15.1%, and news and journalism destinations at 13.4%. Transactional and entertainment-oriented categories showed smaller and, in several cases, statistically indistinguishable changes. The authors note that total visits to these informational categories also declined, not just search-engine referrals specifically, suggesting the lost traffic was not simply picked up by another channel the study could observe. What the paper does and does not claim The authors are explicit about the boundaries of their findings. The measurements describe observable routing patterns in United States desktop browsing, not a judgment about whether ChatGPT provides more or less value to the person using it.
